presentingComplaint: Sudden-onset right-sided weakness and slurred speech 90 minutes ago, with palpitations and a very high blood pressure reading at triage.
history: Witnessed abrupt onset of right facial droop, right arm and leg weakness, and expressive dysphasia while at breakfast; last-known-well precisely documented at 08:10 (95 minutes before arrival). No headache, no vomiting, no preceding trauma. Family also report she felt 'fluttering in the chest' this morning and has been non-adherent with her rate-control medication for a week. Background: hypertension, type 2 diabetes, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation for which she declined anticoagulation last year (fall risk), and a prior transient ischemic attack 2 years ago. On amlodipine, metformin and bisoglurol. The concurrent finding of an irregular tachycardia with markedly elevated BP at triage initially raised concern for a hypertensive emergency or arrhythmia-driven event, but the deficit is clearly focal and abrupt.
examination: Alert, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6) with expressive dysphasia. Right-sided facial weakness (upper-face sparing), right arm drift with 3/5 power, right leg 4/5, right-sided sensory inattention and homonymous field loss. NIHSS 11. Pulse irregularly irregular. Chest clear, no cardiac failure. No neck stiffness, no papilloedema. Capillary glucose 7.2 mmol/L (normal — excludes hypoglycemic mimic).

labs.troponin: mildly elevated (demand), no dynamic ischemic ECG changes

imaging: Non-contrast CT head: no hemorrhage, hyperdense left MCA sign with early loss of insular ribbon; ASPECTS 8. CT angiography: left M1 middle cerebral artery occlusion. CT perfusion: small core with substantial salvageable penumbra.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute ischemic stroke (left MCA, likely cardioembolic from AF)
Hypertensive emergency with encephalopathy (concurrent severe hypertension — but deficit is focal, not global)
finalDiagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke — left M1 MCA occlusion, cardioembolic, in a patient with concurrent AF with rapid ventricular response and reactive severe hypertension
citations: AHA/ASA — Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke — 2019
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Ischemic Stroke
stewardship: Not applicable — non-infective condition; no antimicrobial therapy indicated.
contraindications: BP must be lowered to <185/110 before IV thrombolysis; do not give alteplase/tenecteplase while BP >185/110
Avoid over-aggressive BP reduction in the ischemic penumbra if thrombolysis/thrombectomy not pursued (permissive hypertension)
Do not delay CT/CTA to treat the hypertension or arrhythmia — the focal deficit mandates immediate stroke pathway
No anticoagulation acutely despite AF — risk of hemorrhagic transformation; defer per infarct size
edgeCases: Concurrent AF with RVR and BP 212/108 can mislead toward primary cardiac/hypertensive emergency and delay reperfusion
Within thrombolysis window AND large-vessel occlusion — candidate for IV thrombolysis plus mechanical thrombectomy
Demand troponin rise and rapid AF must not divert the team from time-critical stroke reperfusion
expectedMaiK: Sudden focal neurological deficit with a precise last-known-well, normal glucose, and CT excluding hemorrhage defines acute ischemic stroke; the concurrent AF-with-RVR and severe hypertension are the embolic source and a reactive response, not the primary diagnosis, and must be managed without delaying reperfusion.
expectedNextQuestions: Exact time of last-known-well / symptom onset?
Any anticoagulation, recent surgery, or bleeding — thrombolysis contraindications?
Capillary glucose to exclude hypoglycemic mimic?
Is there large-vessel occlusion on CTA making them a thrombectomy candidate?
expectedInvestigations: CT perfusion / MRI for core-penumbra assessment
regressionAssertions: Must recommend urgent non-contrast CT head before any thrombolysis
Must check capillary glucose to exclude hypoglycemic mimic
Must identify large-vessel occlusion and consider thrombolysis +/- thrombectomy within window
Must NOT treat as primary hypertensive emergency or arrhythmia at the expense of reperfusion
